\title{Numbers or Pixels? What Near-Perfect Rice Variety Scores Depend On}
\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{F20DL Group 16}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Heriot-Watt University}}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We ask whether measured numeric features or raw images classify five rice varieties better when both describe the identical grains. Both sit near the ceiling: a tabular gradient-boosted model reaches \TestAccHgbAllOneZeroSixPct\% test accuracy, a multilayer perceptron \TestAccMlpAllOneZeroSixSeedMeanPct\% (seed mean) and a small convolutional network \TestAccCnnImageSeedMeanPct\% (seed mean). The ceiling hides a late Jasmine capture lot: models that have not seen it miss almost all of it, at high confidence. A small set of size-free features survives the same test. We report what the scores depend on, how our routing flags doubtful grains, and what the evidence does not show.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Rice variety classification has been reported at near-perfect scores from images with convolutional networks~\cite{koklu2021deep} and from measured morphological and colour features~\cite{cinar2021features,cinar2022ml,cinar2019ai}. The two literatures use different grains and different splits, so they cannot be compared directly. Our question is: do measured numeric features or raw images classify five rice varieties better on identical grains, and what do near-perfect scores depend on?

The report is organised as the brief requires: data and analysis, setup, results, a short discussion and a conclusion. We pursue three objectives. \textbf{O1:} compare model families on equal footing, with the same grains, the same splits, tuning on validation only, and one logged test read each. \textbf{O2:} explain the data behind the scores: row-to-image linking, duplicates, a late capture lot and clusters. \textbf{O3:} report what the scores do not show, through disclosures and limits.

\section{Dataset Description and Analysis}
\subsection{Sources}
The Rice Image Dataset holds \DataImagesRaw{} images of five varieties (Arborio, Basmati, Ipsala, Jasmine, Karacadag). The Rice MSC dataset holds 106 numeric feature columns for the same grains: shape, colour statistics and texture measures. Table~\ref{tab:classes} gives the split sizes.

\subsection{Linking and cleaning}
All \LinkRowsRebuilt{} links between table rows and images were rebuilt one-to-one. The median link distance is \LinkMedianTrue{} for true links against \LinkMedianShuffled{} for shuffled links; \CleanLinkDistanceRows{} rows beyond the 99th percentile were kept. \CleanExactDuplicatePairsRows{} exact duplicate pairs, all in Ipsala, were dropped (the later file of each pair), leaving \DataGrainsTotal{} grains. \CleanMissingCellsRows{} rows have `?' cells and are median-imputed inside each model pipeline.

Two checks are reported but nothing is removed. Validity flags mark \CleanValidityColumns{} columns (\CleanValidityCells{} cells in \CleanValidityOutOfRangeRows{} grain rows): the published entropy columns are negative because the published form is $-\sum s^2\ln s^2$ over the non-zero pixel values of the whole image. We treat this as a quirk of the published formula, not as bad data. Robust-$z$ outliers (per class, $|z|>6$) mark \CleanOutlierCells{} cells in \CleanOutliersRobustZSixRows{} rows and are kept.

\subsection{Exploratory analysis}
Classes are balanced. The 15 \texttt{ALLdaub4} columns are near-duplicates of the mean colour columns, so we also use a \texttt{distinct91} set without them. Within Jasmine, a late lot of \LateHoldoutHgbAllOneZeroSixLateAllN{} grains is larger and bluer than early Jasmine (Fig.~\ref{fig:jasmine}): median length is $\times\JasmineLateRatioLength$, width $\times\JasmineLateRatioWidth$, area $\times\JasmineLateRatioArea$, tint $\times\JasmineLateRatioTint$, and \texttt{EXTENT} $\times\JasmineLateRatioExtent$. Its cause is not established. Late grains are spread across all three splits, so overall test accuracy does not measure this shift; the late-lot hold-out (Section~\ref{sec:late}) does.

\subsection{Feature selection}
Mutual information, ANOVA and correlation-cluster pruning select $k=\FeatSelectedK$ columns (validation accuracy \FeatBestValAccPct\%). We tried a grid of $k$ with HGB and logistic regression and took the smallest $k$ within one tenth of a point of each model's best validation accuracy, then the larger of the two. The authors' own top five shape features differ~\cite{cinar2021features}: \texttt{ROUNDNESS}, \texttt{COMPACTNESS}, \texttt{SHAPEFACTOR\_3}, \texttt{ASPECT\_RATIO}, \texttt{ECCENTRICITY}. Our columns: \footnotesize\texttt{\FeatSelectedNames}.\normalsize

\subsection{Clustering}
As the unsupervised and generative view, we fit $k$-means and Gaussian mixtures (GMM) for $k$ from two to ten on a twenty-component PCA of all106 (cumulative variance \ClusterPcaCumVarAllOneZeroSixPct\%), train grains only, and score on validation with ARI, NMI, silhouette and BIC. The best GMM uses $k=\ClusterBestGmmAllOneZeroSixK$ (ARI \ClusterBestGmmAllOneZeroSixARIVal); the best $k$-means uses $k=\ClusterBestKmeansAllOneZeroSixK$ (ARI \ClusterBestKmeansAllOneZeroSixARIVal). On the size-free set the best GMM is lower (ARI \ClusterBestGmmSizefreeTwoTwoARIVal), again showing that size carries part of the variety signal (Fig.~\ref{fig:cluster}). The GMM silhouette at its best $k$ is \ClusterGmmAllOneZeroSixKFiveSilhouette. At $k$ equal to six, $k$-means puts a share \ClusterLateKmeansAllOneZeroSixShare{} of the late lot into one cluster, of purity \ClusterLateKmeansAllOneZeroSixPurity: the unlabelled structure already separates the lot.

\section{Experimental Setup}
Splits are stratified by class and lot, 70/15/15 into train, validation and test with seed zero (Table~\ref{tab:classes}). Hyperparameters are tuned on validation only. We then froze the code and a results hash, and made exactly \TestReadsCount{} logged single test reads.

\textbf{Feature sets.} \texttt{all106}: all columns. \texttt{distinct91}: without the near-duplicates. \texttt{selected}: the pruned set above. \texttt{shape16}: shape columns. \texttt{colour90}: colour columns. \texttt{sizefree7}: seven shape ratios. \texttt{sizefree22}: those plus mean colour columns.

\textbf{Models.} Baselines: logistic regression, $k$-nearest neighbours, perceptron, naive Bayes, a Gaussian-mixture classifier, decision trees (including depth four) and histogram gradient boosting (HGB). Neural: an MLP on all106 and a small CNN (SmallCNN) on images, three seeds each. Routing chain: HGB answers when confident, the CNN takes grains HGB declines, and the rest are flagged unsure or unfamiliar.

\textbf{Neural settings.} The MLP takes all106, median-imputed and standardised on train; its best validation configuration has hidden layers of \NeuralMlpHiddenOne{} and \NeuralMlpHiddenTwo{} units with ReLU, dropout \NeuralMlpDropout{} and learning rate \NeuralMlpLr. The SmallCNN takes the whole 250\,px crop resized uniformly to 128\,px and scaled by the train channel mean and spread; it has four blocks of $3\times3$ convolution, batch normalisation, ReLU and $2\times2$ max-pooling, with base width \NeuralCnnWidth{} doubling per block, global average pooling, dropout \NeuralCnnDropout{} and a linear layer to five classes. Both use AdamW (weight decay $10^{-4}$, cosine schedule) and cross-entropy; the CNN learning rate is \NeuralCnnLr{} and it uses horizontal and vertical flips only (no zoom, crop or colour jitter, so size and tint stay measurable). Table~\ref{tab:nn} lists the rest. The CNN trains on the Apple MPS GPU, the MLP on CPU; seeds are zero, one and two. Settings were tuned on validation, with the CNN grid run on a small train subset.

\begin{table}[t]

\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
 & MLP & SmallCNN\\
\midrule

\textbf{Baseline settings.} Each baseline's grid point is chosen on validation macro-F1. For all106 the choices are: decision tree depth \ParamTreeAllOneZeroSixMaxDepth, $k$NN with $k=\ParamKnnAllOneZeroSixNNeighbors$, logistic regression $C=\ParamLogregAllOneZeroSixC$, GMM classifier with \ParamGmmAllOneZeroSixNComponents{} components, and HGB with learning rate \ParamHgbAllOneZeroSixLearningRate, \ParamHgbAllOneZeroSixMaxIter{} iterations and \ParamHgbAllOneZeroSixMaxLeafNodes{} leaves. As a leakage guard we also ran each model on shuffled training labels: the best validation accuracy was \ControlBaselineMaxValAccPct\% over \ControlBaselineRows{} baseline rows (\ControlMlpValAccPct\% for the MLP, \ControlCnnValAccPct\% for the CNN), and the stop rule (the ceiling, not a band around chance; see the disclosures) was not triggered.

\textbf{Metrics.} Accuracy and macro-F1 (classes are balanced, but per-class failure matters), Wilson intervals at the ninety-five percent level, and exact McNemar tests on paired predictions. The family fixed in advance is three pairs at seed zero (HGB against CNN as the primary pair, HGB against MLP, MLP against CNN) with Holm correction across the three; seeds one and two repeat the same three tests as a check.

\subsection{Neural models}
The MLP makes \TestErrorsMlpAllOneZeroSixSeedZero, \TestErrorsMlpAllOneZeroSixSeedOne{} and \TestErrorsMlpAllOneZeroSixSeedTwo{} test errors on its three seeds (seed mean \TestAccMlpAllOneZeroSixSeedMeanPct\%, sd \TestAccMlpAllOneZeroSixSeedMeanSdPct{} points). The CNN makes between \TestErrMinCnnImage{} and \TestErrMaxCnnImage{} errors (seed mean \TestAccCnnImageSeedMeanPct\%, sd \TestAccCnnImageSeedMeanSdPct{} points), so its seeds differ widely. Fig.~\ref{fig:curves} shows why this is plausible: the CNN validation loss jumps from epoch to epoch and early stopping ends the three runs at different points, while the MLP curves are smooth. We do not claim this is the cause. Fig.~\ref{fig:conf} shows the test confusions.

\subsection{Paired tests}
HGB against the MLP shows no significant difference on any seed (Holm-adjusted exact McNemar $p=\McNemarHgbAllOneZeroSixVsMlpAllOneZeroSixSeedZeroPHolm$, $\McNemarHgbAllOneZeroSixVsMlpAllOneZeroSixSeedOnePHolm$ and $\McNemarHgbAllOneZeroSixVsMlpAllOneZeroSixSeedTwoPHolm$). Tabular against CNN differed significantly for seeds zero and two (Holm $p=\McNemarHgbAllOneZeroSixVsCnnImageSeedZeroPHolm$ and $\McNemarHgbAllOneZeroSixVsCnnImageSeedTwoPHolm$) but not for seed one ($p=\McNemarHgbAllOneZeroSixVsCnnImageSeedOnePHolm$). The CNN gap therefore depends on the seed.

\subsection{Routing}
The routing chain works in three steps. HGB answers a grain when its confidence is above its floor; the CNN takes grains HGB declined, if its own confidence is above its floor; a table-side and an image-side familiarity gate flag grains unlike anything seen as unfamiliar. Grains neither model will answer are marked unsure. For seed zero, the chain answers a share \RouteSeedZeroAnsweredTotalShare{} of the \TestN{} test grains with \RouteSeedZeroAnsweredTotalErrors{} errors (accuracy \RouteSeedZeroAnsweredTotalAccPct\%). The unsure share is \RouteSeedZeroUnsureShare{} and the unfamiliar share \RouteSeedZeroUnfamiliarShare. At a ninety-five percent coverage point the chain's accuracy is \RouteSeedZeroChainErrAtNineFiveCoverageAccPct\%. Floors were set in-sample on validation (see the disclosures), so these routing figures are optimistic.

\subsection{Grey-world tint arm}
This arm asks whether the CNNs trained with the late lot lean on its blue tint. On the \GreyN{} late-lot test grains, grey-world colour correction (which removes the overall tint of an image) takes CNN recall from \GreyCnnRawSeedMeanPct\% (seed mean, uncorrected, same loading path) to \GreyCnnGreySeedMeanPct\%. So the corrected images are no longer recognised, but that alone does not show that colour is the reason. The pre-set check that the correction gain does not track grain area passed only for Arborio. For Jasmine the largest absolute correlation was \GreyGainAreaJasmineMaxAbs, so there colour cannot be separated from size.

\section{Brief Discussion}

\textbf{Decision trees in practice.} A depth-four tree reaches \TestAccTreeFourAllOneZeroSixPct\% test accuracy with rules a grading station can read and audit (Fig.~\ref{fig:tree}). Its top splits use \texttt{SHAPEFACTOR\_3}, then \texttt{MAJOR\_AXIS} and \texttt{PERIMETER}: pixel-scale size measures. A change of camera scale, or a larger lot such as the late one, moves grains across such thresholds. A practical use is an interpretable first stage with a familiarity check, recalibrated per camera.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{baselines_tree_depth4.png}
\caption{Depth-four decision tree.}\label{fig:tree}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Numbers versus pixels.} On identical grains the tabular models are at least as accurate as the CNN on every seed; the gap is significant for two of the three CNN seeds, and the MLP and HGB do not differ significantly. The near-perfect scores lean on size, which fails when the lot changes; size-free features trade a little accuracy for robustness.

\textbf{What near-perfect means.} On \TestN{} test grains, HGB makes \TestErrorsHgbAllOneZeroSix{} errors, about \ErrPerTenThousandHgb{} per ten thousand grains; the MLP seeds make \ErrPerTenThousandMlpMin{} to \ErrPerTenThousandMlpMax{}, the CNN seeds \ErrPerTenThousandCnnMin{} to \ErrPerTenThousandCnnMax, and the depth-four tree \ErrPerTenThousandTreeFour. HGB and the MLP differ by a handful of grains and their Wilson intervals in Table~\ref{tab:head} overlap; the depth-four tree is clearly lower, and the CNN depends on its seed. What matters more than the last decimal is whether a model's confidence is calibrated and whether it can say a grain is unfamiliar: the late lot was missed at high confidence, which no test accuracy reveals.

\textbf{Limitations.} One dataset, one source and camera; the cause of the late lot is not established; validation contains late grains; routing is calibrated in-sample; GPU nondeterminism makes seeds drift.


\section{Conclusion}
On identical grains, the tabular models are at least as accurate as the CNN on every seed, the gap is significant for two of three CNN seeds, and the MLP and HGB do not differ significantly. The near-perfect scores depend on size, and a late Jasmine lot that unseen models miss at high confidence exposes it, while size-free features survive. Future work: data from several lots, size normalisation, and an external camera.
